The GrowthCred field guide

How can private AI help with POPIA?

Private AI can help you control where business information is processed and who can reach it. That can reduce some data exposure. It does not make your business POPIA-compliant by itself. You still need a lawful, secure and well-governed workflow. Your setup must fit the information you use and the job you need done. You should assess the workflow before choosing the setup.

By Phila Ngwenya · Published 13 October 2026

Start with the information, not the hardware

POPIA applies to personal information. Your client documents may also carry confidentiality, contractual or professional duties. List the information in the task, its purpose, who may use it and what the output will do. You need to include the connected tools too.

Then decide what the system needs. Remove information the task doesn't need. Set who can access the files and outputs. Decide what gets kept, for how long and who checks the work. You choose the purpose and the people who may use it.

What private AI can change

A private setup can be designed so documents are processed on equipment inside your business rather than sent to an outside AI provider. That gives you a different place to set access, retention and operating controls. You can design those controls around your work.

But location is only one part of the picture. A private system can still expose data through weak permissions, poor security, unnecessary collection, unsafe backups or a badly designed workflow. A system inside your office is not automatically a safe system. You still have to check the full setup.

Free guide

The AI Implementation Guide helps you give a system useful business context. Start there, then decide which information the task is allowed to use.

What the law still asks you to do

Section 19 requires reasonable technical and organisational measures to protect personal information. Sections 20 and 21 cover people or operators processing it on your behalf, including written security commitments for operators. You need to review those arrangements.

If a workflow transfers personal information to a third party in another country, check section 72 and the actual arrangements. On-premise processing may reduce one transfer. It doesn't settle every transfer made by connected tools, support services, backups or people. You should map each route the information takes.

Keep a human responsible for outputs. Review the result before it reaches a client or changes a record. Agree what the system may do, what it must not do and how someone stops it. Your team needs to know who takes that decision.

A sensible first test

Choose one recurring task. Use a sample without personal information. Map the source files, access, output, reviewer and failure route. Then test the same task with approved information only after the responsible people have signed off. You can start with a fictional example.

Measure whether the process improved. Keep a record of the controls you chose. Recheck them when the data, provider or workflow changes. You should revisit the controls when the work changes too.

Private is a design choice. Compliance is the work around it.

Frequently asked questions

Does on-premise AI make us POPIA-compliant?+
No. It can change where some processing happens and help you control access. You still need to assess purpose, lawful processing, minimisation, safeguards, operators, retention and any transfers for the whole workflow.
Does private AI mean no data leaves the building?+
That depends on the complete design and operating arrangements, including connected tools, support, backups and access. Define and verify the data flows before making that claim about a system.
What should we review before a private AI pilot?+
Choose the information and purpose, approved users, access controls, retention, security measures, output review, operator agreements, transfer routes and failure process. Ask your privacy or legal adviser to assess your obligations.
